author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Referred to the interior section: draft rules reorganising the Paris National Guard. […]”

tweet: I Referred to the interior section: draft rules reorganising the Paris National guard. The capital's defence is reorganised.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Whereas Brigade Chief Dupuy, dead arms in hand at Cairo, commanded the 32nd through five campaigns. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Dupuy died commanding the 32nd through five campaigns: honored. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Considérant que le chef de brigade Dupuy, mort les armes à la main au Caire, a commandé pendant cinq campagnes la 32e demi-brigade.
tweet: I whereas Brigade chief dupuy, dead arms in hand at Cairo, commanded the through five campaigns. The fallen hero is honoured.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am satisfied with your conduct in the 8th division. Enlighten the people; let all citizens feel that parties and strife are past. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Parties are over: enlighten the people, set everything in motion. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je suis satisfait de la conduite que vous tenez dans la 8e division. Éclairez le peuple, faites sentir à tous les citoyens que le temps des partis et des déchirements est passé.
tweet: I am satisfied with your conduct in the division. Enlighten the people; Let all citizens feel that parties and strife are past. The division commander earns my confidence.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tell me Pichegru's conduct abroad since 18 Fructidor Year V. Truth is wanted, not calumny. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Truth not calumny: what did Pichegru do abroad since Fructidor? Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je suis chargé de vous demander quelle a été la conduite de Pichegru en pays étranger, depuis le 18 fructidor an V. C'est la vérité qu'on veut connaître, et non la calomnie.
tweet: Tell me Pichegru's conduct abroad since 18 Fructidor Year V. Truth is wanted, not calumny. The Consul demands facts, not slander.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You asked 15,000 men. Consul Bonaparte charges me to answer by extraordinary courier. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: 15,000 men demanded and more: courier extraordinary. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous avez demandé 15,000 hommes. Le Consul Bonaparte vient de recevoir votre lettre et me charge de vous écrire par courrier extraordinaire.
tweet: You asked 15,000 men. Consul Bonaparte charges me to answer by extraordinary courier. The First Consul directs the war effort.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Chouan bands gather in Orne. The First Consul complains of hearing nothing from you. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Chouan bands in Orne: what are you doing, what are your troops doing? Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Des rassemblements de chouans existent dans le département de l'Orne. Le Premier Consul se plaint de n'avoir pas encore entendu parler de vous.
tweet: Chouan bands gather in Orne. The First Consul complains of hearing nothing from you. The rebellion in the west demands attention.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The war minister will report at once the clothing administration's state. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Report at once: clothing, linen, shoes, harness administration. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le ministre de la guerre me fera connaître le plus tôt possible l'état actuel de l'administration de l'habillement.
tweet: I the War minister will report at once the clothing administration's state. The Consul demands accountability in supply.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The First Consul saw with indignation chouans settled at Saint-Jean de Margon. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Chouans at Saint-Jean: indignation that Ramefroy's letter sufficed. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le Premier Consul a vu avec indignation qu'on ait laissé établir les chouans à Saint-Jean de Margon.
tweet: I the first Consul saw with indignation chouans settled at saint-jean de margon. The rebellion in the west will not be tolerated.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order General Gardanne and all England-army officers embarked by the 24th. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: England army officers to embark by the 24th, no delay. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous ordonnerez sur-le-champ au général de division Gardanne et aux autres officiers de l'armée d'Angleterre d'être rendus le 24 du courant.
tweet: I Order general gardanne and all England-army officers embarked by the. The expeditionary force must sail on schedule.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We expect at each moment 1,500,000 francs drawn from Holland, which will be forwarded to you. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To Masséna: We expect at each moment 1,500,000 francs drawn from Holland, which will be forwarded to you.
voice: @massena We expect at each moment 1,500,000 francs drawn from Holland, which will be forwarded to you
tweet: I am glad to see order restored in your army. Holland million and a half comes to you; Vendée is nearly pacified, and Brune has beaten little Georges.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “This hymn must coatain things applicable to all the circumstances of war, and propound the idea that peace follows in the train of victory. u BONAPARTE.'' It is impossible to read the following letter without feelings of astonishment: […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To his brother Lucien: War hymn ordered.
tweet: Minister — have Lebrun and Rouget write me a battle hymn to a known tune, Marseillaise or Chant du Départ. It must sing of every circumstance of war, and that peace marches behind victory.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I was very well satisfied with him Shall we have peace } Shall we have war? However this may be, the Emperor treats us with the greatest politeness. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To Marshal Brune: I have received your despatch of the i ith Ventose.
voice: I was very well satisfied with him Shall we have peace } Shall we have war?
tweet: I have seen Georges — a sturdy Breton we may yet turn to the country account — and Chatillon dined with me today. I am well satisfied with both; and the Emperor treats us with utmost politeness.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That the intention of his Catholic Majesty in leaving fifteen vessels at Brest was not to render them useless to the advantage and glory of the two nations; that consequently the First Consul desires orders may be given to Admiral Gravina by telegraph to second the sortie of the French fleet. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To his foreign minister Talleyrand: That the intention of his Catholic Majesty in leaving fifteen vessels at Brest was not to render them useless to the advantage and glory of the two nations.
tweet: Bruix lies blockaded at Brest by twenty-one English against his seventeen French and Gravina fifteen Spaniards — humiliation for two nations by an inferior force. I have telegraphed: put to sea, chase them.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will inform citizen Otto, the French Commissioner in London, that the Government will consent to the exchange of General Don for Napper Tandy and his companions; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: You will inform citizen Otto, the French Commissioner in London, that the Government will consent to the exchange of General Don for Napper Tandy and his companions.
voice: @talleyrand You will inform citizen Otto, the French Commissioner in London, that the Government will consent to the exchange of General Don for Napper Tandy and his companions
tweet: Tell Otto in London from me: we will trade General Don for Napper Tandy and companions — or Hermann, Don and Mack for Colli, Perignon and Grouchy. Threatening our prisoners captivity shames Newton nation; prisoners answer for no government, and France never retaliates.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Consuls of the Republic desire you will inform the managers of the different theatres that no dramatic work ought to be accepted without your permission. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his brother Lucien: The Consuls of the Republic desire you will inform the managers of the different theatres that no dramatic work ought to be accepted without your permission.
voice: @lucien The Consuls of the Republic desire you will inform the managers of the different theatres that no dramatic work ought to be accepted without your permission
tweet: No play reaches the stage without your leave, and I hold Public Instruction answerable for every immoral piece. I would also enjoy seeing the couplet about me cut from the Tableau des Sabines.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “When you receive this letter the gallant army of the East will have re-entered the ports of the Republic after having left in Egypt immortal traces of its glorious works. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To Kléber in Egypt: When you receive this letter the gallant army of the East will have re-entered the ports of the Republic after having left in Egypt immortal traces of its glorious works.
tweet: When you read this, the army of the East will be home, leaving immortal traces in Egypt. And you, who justified my choice in giving you command — I know your satisfaction at the prospect of return.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “By letters I have received it appears that Desaix, Menou, Davoust, and several other generals of courage were opposed to the evacuation of Egypt. All that I say here is intended for you. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Consuls Of The Republic, Lausanne, 1800-05-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Lausanne. To The Consuls Of The Republic: By letters I have received it appears that Desaix, Menou, Davoust, and several other generals of courage were opposed to the evacuation of Egypt.
voice: @republic All that I say here is intended for you
tweet: Print my letter whole — let the public know Egypt as I left it, against England exaggerations. Two years, great battles, and the army not diminished a fifth; no plague this year. Abandoning it is infamous.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We are struggling against ice, snow, storms, and avalanches. The St. Bernard, astonished to see so many persons crossing it, throws obstacles in our way. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Consuls Of The Republic, Martigny, 1800-05-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Martigny. To The Consuls Of The Republic: The St. Bernard, astonished to see so many persons crossing it, throws obstacles in our way.
voice: We are struggling against ice, snow, storms, and avalanches
tweet: Your letter on Lucien wife death — she suffered long. Meanwhile we fight ice, snow and avalanches; the Bernard himself resists us, yet a third of my guns are over. In three days the whole army crosses.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “On the 5 th June, Bonaparte pronounced a long allocution to the clergy of Milan. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Headquarters. To Fouchfi: I am assured that Georges has returned from England.
tweet: I hear Georges is back from England — take him dead or alive, with Frotté father in the Orne. Spare nothing.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have just received your letter of the 22nd Floreal. I beg you will have the inclosed printed at length in the official journal, for it is well for the public to know the situation of the army of Egypt when I left it, and how exaggerated are the reports made by the agents of England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Second Italian campaign opens: First Consul writing to his colleagues. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: I have just received your letter of the Floreal.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “But how came it that 16,00.0 or 18,000 Frenchmen were afraid of 30,000 Turks? Six thousand men would have been sufficient to have beaten them, captured their guns and camels, &c. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To his rival Moreau: But how came it that 16,00.0 or 18,000 Frenchmen were afraid of 30,000 Turks?
tweet: I was leaving for Geneva when the telegraph sang your victory — glory, three times glory! Italy is critical, Massena locked in Genoa — I salute you affectionately.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Soldiers: When we began our march, one department of France was in the hands of the enemy. Consternation pervaded the south of the Repubhc. You advanced. Joy and hope in our country have succeeded to consternation and fear. The enemy, terror - struck, seeks only to regain his frontiers. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Marengo eve proclamation.
tweet: Soldiers: When we began our march, one department of France was in the hands of the enemy. Consternation pervaded the south of the Republic. You advanced. Joy and hope in our country have succeeded to consternation and fear.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sire: — It is on the field of battle, amid the sufferings of a multitude of wounded, and surrounded by fifteen thousand corpses, that I beseech your Majesty to listen to the voice of humanity, and not to suffer two brave nations to cut each other's throats for interests not their own. […]”
sourceTitle: Letter to the Emperor of Austria, 1800-06-01
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: To Austria, on the field.
tweet: Sire, amid my wounded and fifteen thousand corpses I beg you hear humanity: let not two brave nations cut throats for others' interests. I write from the field itself.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I shall arrive unexpectedly in Paris. It is not my intention to have triumphal arches or any kind of ceremony. I have too good an opinion of myself to care about such nonsense. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To his brother Lucien: I shall arrive unexpectedly in Paris.
voice: I shall arrive unexpectedly in Paris
tweet: I arrive unexpectedly — no arches, no ceremonies. I think too well of myself for such nonsense; public satisfaction is my only triumph.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write to General Kleber that when the news of the capitulation arrived, the Brest squadron was about to sail with 4,000 troops and war stores; that we have only just learned the capitulation has been broken, and that he has reconquered Egypt; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: After Marengo: Kléber, Egypt, and broken capitulations. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: Write to General Kleber that when the news of the capitulation arrived, the Brest squadron was about to sail with 4,000 troops and war stores; we have only just learned the capitulation has been broken, and he has reconquered Egypt.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write to General Kleber that when the news of the capitulation arrived, the Brest squadron was about to sail with 4,000 troops and war stores”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To Carnot: Write to General Kleber that when the news of the capitulation arrived, the Brest squadron was about to sail with 4,000 troops and war stores.
tweet: I write to General Kleber: when capitulation news arrived, the Brest squadron was about to sail with 4,000 troops and war stores; the capitulation was broken, and he has reconquered Egypt.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “BULLETIN TO THE ARMY. "Milan, izrdjune 1800. 'A Turkish ambassador coming from Leghorn on board an English frigate has arrived at Genoa. He has informed Admiral Keith of the deplorable condition of the Grand Vizier who has been driven back across the desert. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To his chief of staff Berthier: A Turkish ambassador coming from Leghorn on board an English frigate has arrived at Genoa.
tweet: Send me Paris two best virtuosos for an Italian duo at the summer festival, all expenses paid — Mesdames Billington and Grassini.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg you will invite two of the best virtuosos to go to Paris in order to sing a duo in Italian at the fete of the 14th July. You will give them all that is necessary for their voyage, &c. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Virtuosos for the national fête — war administration as usual. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.
tweet: I beg you will invite two of the best virtuosos to go to Paris to sing a duo in Italian at the fete of the. You will give them all necessary for their voyage. Madame Billington and Madame Grassini are the chosen singers.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I congratulate you, General, on the brilliant results of your campaign. We are expecting every moment an answer from Vienna, and if it does not arrive in a few days we shall recommence hostilities in Italy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To his rival Moreau: We are expecting every moment an answer from Vienna, and if it does not arrive in a few days we shall recommence hostilities in Italy.
voice: @moreau I congratulate you, General, on the brilliant results of your campaign
tweet: I congratulate you on a brilliant campaign. We await Vienna answer daily — silence means war in Italy. Meanwhile Batavians and French mass beyond Mayence, and my second reserve forms.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In the year VIII. (1800) an attempt was made to re-establish the Academy on its ancient footing, and the idea was encouraged by Lucien Bonaparte, then Minister of the Interior. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To his brother Lucien: That they ought to know that it was dissolved by a law of the Republic.
tweet: Tell them from me: no French Academy exists — the law dissolved it, and the Institute stands in its place. Citizens may form a literary society, unnamed, with republican rules like the Arts Lyceum.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Command of his centre. He has made the most favourable report of your operations. I see by your letter that you are zealous to acquire glory; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To General Suchet: Command of his centre. He has made the most favourable report of your operations.
voice: @suchet I see by your letter that you are zealous to acquire glory
tweet: I am Glad Massena gave you his centre — his report of your operations delights me. I see your zeal for glory; that is the road. Count on my esteem and friendship.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Consuls have been informed that the citizen Foissac-Latour has returned from Austria and dishonours the French uniform by wearing it. Let him know that he ceased to belong to the service of the Republic the day he basely surrendered the citadel of Mantua. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To Carnot: The Consuls have been informed that the citizen Foissac-Latour has returned from Austria and dishonours the French uniform by wearing it.
tweet: I am told Foissac-Latour skulks back in our uniform since basely yielding Mantua. He answers to public opinion for that stain — my Government is done with him.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is my intention to send General Berthier to Spain without any apparent diplomatic title. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: It is my intention to send General Berthier to Spain without any apparent diplomatic title.
tweet: I Send Berthier to Spain with no title — letters from you to Urquijo, from me to the king. Tuscany for Parma Duke against Louisiana and twelve warships; rouse Spain against Portugal; survey her ports; corn for Malta from Barcelona.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have already informed you that you have been called by the esteem and confidence of the Consuls to the chief command of the forces in Germany. The modesty with which you refused to accept this important command has proved an additional motive for conferring it upon you. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To his rival Moreau: I have already informed you that you have been called by the esteem and confidence of the Consuls to the chief command of the forces in Germany.
voice: @moreau I have already informed you that you have been called by the esteem and confidence of the Consuls to the chief command of the forces in Germany
tweet: I give you Germany with the Consuls esteem and confidence — your modest refusal only confirms you. Vienna delays may break the armistice any hour; Angereau is yours, with full liberty.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “(words omitted). History will not forget this. *' I am not insensible to the misfortunes of your family. (more words omitted). I shall contribute with pleasure to the pleasantness and tranquillity of your retreat. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Comte De Provence, Paris, 1800-09-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To The Comte De Provence: History will not forget this. *' I am not insensible to the misfortunes of your family.
voice: @provence I am not insensible to the misfortunes of your family
tweet: I have your letter, and thank you for its flatteries. But do not return — you would march over 100,000 corpses. Sacrifice yourself to France repose; history will remember. I feel for your family and will sweeten your retreat.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The courier who was expected has returned from Vienna, bringing no positive answer. This proves that the Court of Vienna wishes to gain the winter. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To Carnot: This proves that the Court of Vienna wishes to gain the winter.
tweet: Telegraph Strasbourg for a courier to Moreau: Vienna answers nothing, which means she wants winter. Tell their general from me that we restart hostilities — his Emperor refused St. Julien preliminaries.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The intrigues of the faction opposed to peace have induced the Emperor to refuse his ratification”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To The Public Functionaries: The intrigues of the faction opposed to peace have induced the Emperor to refuse his ratification.
tweet: I the preliminaries of peace were signed at Paris on the Thermidor ( ) between Talleyrand and count st. Julien, ratified by the Consuls. Duroc carried them to Vienna. The intrigues of the faction opposed to peace induced the Emperor to refuse ratification.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I pity those who have not sufficient virtue to second you in your noble resolution, and whose courage has failed them. They will find in France that contempt due to men who, no matter what their services, are deficient in the necessary amount of constancy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To General Menou: I pity those who have not sufficient virtue to second you in your noble resolution, and whose courage has failed them.
tweet: Ganteaume brings this. Peace with America, Algiers, Tunis; fair hopes everywhere. The honourably returned are esteemed — but I pity men without constancy for your noble resolve.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You must show no pity in such cases. If any revolts take place in remote corners, make severe examples. All foreign people but especially Italians require to be dealt with severely from time to time. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To Marshal Brune: All foreign people but especially Italians require to be dealt with severely from time to time.
voice: @brune You must show no pity in such cases
tweet: I expect Dupard with two and a half millions in gold. Make Arezzo pay for storming — assaulted towns pay, no pity. Revolt anywhere gets severe examples; Italians, of all foreigners, need severity at times.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you the Citizen Jerome Bonaparte to serve his apprenticeship in the marine. You know he will have to be kept in order so as to make up for lost time. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To Rear-Admiral Ganteaume: I send you the Citizen Jerome Bonaparte to serve his apprenticeship in the marine.
voice: @ganteaume I send you the Citizen Jerome Bonaparte to serve his apprenticeship in the marine
tweet: I send you young Jérôme for His Sea apprenticeship — keep him in order, make up his lost time, exact every duty. Tell me soon he has succeeded.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I should not regret expending 40,000 francs in this affair.BONAPARTE" On the same day Talleyrand was ordered to see that every vessel which tried to reach Egypt carried 1,000 muskets, 10,000 cannon balls, 250 pairs of pistols, 250 sabres, and medical stores. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To his interior minister Chaptal: On the same day Talleyrand was ordered to see that every vessel which tried to reach Egypt carried 1,000 muskets, 10,000 cannon balls, 250 pairs of pistols, 250 sabres…
voice: I should not regret expending 40,000 francs in this affair
tweet: Send Cairo a company of French comedians — an idle, prosperous army needs theatre, even as politics. Forty thousand francs I do not grudge. And Talleyrand: every Egypt-bound hull carries muskets, cannon, pistols, sabres, stores.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That we shall evacuate it only on the conclusion of a general peace, and that it is in the interest of the Porte to resume its ancient relations with France. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: One afternoon saves the Consulate. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: That we shall evacuate it only on the conclusion of a general peace, and that it is in the interest of the Porte to resume its ancient relations with France.
tweet: I want a letter to the Grand Seigneur through his ambassador here. Lay Europe before him — England alone blocks Egypt evacuation, which waits only on General peace. It is the Porte interest to resume with France.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They counted upon the snow and ice; they were not yet acquainted with you. *' I salute you affectionately, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his rival Moreau: They were not yet acquainted with you.
tweet: Your letter is here — thanks for the Nivose tidings. I followed your splendid manoeuvres with delight; you surpass yourself again. These obstinate Austrians counted on snow and ice, and never met you.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Legislators, the Republic triumphs. Hohenlinden's victory resounded through Europe. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Hohenlinden resounds through Europe. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Législateurs, la République triomphe. La victoire de Hohenlinden a retenti dans toute l'Europe.
tweet: I legislators, the Republic triumphs. Hohenlinden's victory resounded through Europe. The French arms have prevailed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The navy minister shall arrest Citizen Tallien, charged with quitting Egypt without passport. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Tallien arrested for quitting Egypt without passport. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le ministre de la marine fera mettre en arrestation le citoyen Tallien, prévenu d'avoir quitté l'Égypte sans passe-port.
tweet: I the navy minister shall arrest citizen tallien, charged with quitting Egypt without passport. The deserter from the East faces justice.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Hand M. de Muzquiz a letter complaining of changed preparations against Portugal. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Spain pressed to make Portugal act against England. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de remettre à M. de Muzquiz une lettre dans laquelle vous vous plaindrez des changements dans les préparatifs contre le Portugal.
tweet: I hand m. De muzquiz a letter complaining of changed preparations against Portugal. The diplomatic pressure on Lisbon continues.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write General Menou that no serious Egypt landing can happen but at Aboukir. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Aboukir the only serious landing: warn Menou. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je désire que vous écriviez au général Menou, pour lui faire connaître qu'un débarquement en Égypte ne peut avoir sérieusement lieu qu'à Aboukir.
tweet: I Write General Menou that no serious Egypt landing can happen but at Aboukir. The landing site is fixed by geography.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “To send four ships of the line and two frigates, with 2,000 soldiers, to Trinidad; and to arm all the vessels it possessed at Cadiz, Barcelona, and Carthagena, in order to attack Mahon. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: And to arm all the vessels it possessed at Cadiz, Barcelona, and Carthagena, in order to attack Mahon.
tweet: I want Madrid told: Russia writes friendly, France and Russia will decide Prussia, cutting England from the Continent. Then France, Spain and Holland strike together — Ireland, Brazil, Surinam.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I thank you for your news of the extraordinary 3 Nivôse event. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Thanks for Hohenlinden — and the infernal machine survived. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous remercie de ce que vous me dites sur l'événement extraordinaire du 3 nivôse.
tweet: I thank you for your news of the extraordinary 3 Nivose event. The Consul acknowledges the report.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Forty men leave Bicêtre tomorrow for Orléans, thence to embark at Nantes. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Forty men from Bicêtre to Orléans to Nantes, then by sea. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Quarante individus partent demain de Bicêtre pour Orléans, et de là se rendront à Nantes, où ils seront embarqués.
tweet: I forty men leave bicetre tomorrow for orleans, thence to embark at Nantes. The conscripts move to the embarkation port.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Brune putting Tuscany under your orders seems to me extremely wise. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Brune put Tuscany under Murat: wise confidence. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: La mesure prise par le général Brune, de mettre la Toscane sous vos ordres, me paraît extrêmement sage.
tweet: Brune putting Tuscany under your orders seems to me extremely wise. The command structure in Italy is rationalised.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A law will let Ajaccio sell lands to bring water. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Ajaccio may sell lands for water; old forts demolished. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Une loi va autoriser la commune d'Ajaccio à vendre une partie de ses biens pour se procurer de l'eau.
tweet: I a law will Let Ajaccio sell lands to bring water. The birthplace of the Consul gets its aqueduct.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Combis's mission: remind Santo Domingo's people the land is now French. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Combis mission: remind Spanish Santo Domingo it is French. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le principal but de la mission du citoyen Combis à Saint-Domingue est de faire souvenir aux habitants que ce pays est désormais français.
tweet: I combis's mission: remind santo domingo's people the land is now French. The colony remembers its allegiance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Toussaint Louverture, amid revolutionary storms, saved France a great colony by prudence and courage. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Toussaint praised: prudence and courage saved the colony. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Toussaint Louverture, au milieu des orages de la révolution, est parvenu, par sa prudence et son courage, à sauver à la France une grande colonie.
tweet: I general toussaint louverture, amid revolutionary storms, saved France a great colony by prudence and courage. The black general earns the consul's respect.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Draft a treaty for Helvetia to cede all Valais to Brigg. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Valais to the Léman department: treaty with Helvetia. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de préparer un projet de traité avec l'Helvétie, pour qu'elle nous cède tout le Valais jusqu'à Brigg.
tweet: I draft a treaty for helvetia to cede all Valais to brigg. The Swiss cantons yield territory to France.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Yesterday a Russian courier arrived in fifteen days with an extremely friendly letter. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: A friendly Russian letter in fifteen days: Paul melts. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Hier est arrivé de Russie un courrier qui a fait la route en quinze jours; il m'a apporté une lettre extrêmement amicale.
tweet: I yesterday a Russian courier arrived in fifteen days with an extremely friendly letter. The czar's overture is welcome.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They must stir themselves at Madrid. Make the z 2 340 thp: correspondence of napoleon. Spaniards feel how shameful it is for the Spanish monarchy that two vessels should blockade seven in the port of Cadiz. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Make the z 2 340 thp: correspondence of napoleon. Spaniards feel how shameful it is for the Spanish monarchy that two vessels should blockade seven in the port of Cadiz.
tweet: I Send St. Cyr marching — Tell Madrid, but keep Ganteaume secret: seven ships, 4,000 men for Egypt. Shame them: two ships blockade seven of ours at Cadiz. Are these Castile conquerors?

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It will be remarked that Portugal, instead of 8,000,000, was now called upon to pay from 15,000,000 to 20,000,000 francs. It becomes difficult to follow all the territorial combinations in which the First Consul indulged. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To his foreign minister Talleyrand: By a secret treaty concluded with Spain, she is to give us six ships of the line As for Portugal, independently of the conditions inserted in the treaty…
tweet: By secret treaty Spain gives six ships. From Portugal I demand 15 to 20 millions, four ships of the line and the frigate that blockaded me at Alexandria — a lesson to small powers. Tuscany and Elba pieces to settle with Naples.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am going to assemble, as your Majesty appears to wish, 300 or 400 gun launches in the ports of Flanders, where I shall concentrate an army. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Emperor Of Russia, I'jth, 1801-02-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: I'Jth. To Tsar Alexander: I am going to assemble, as your Majesty appears to wish, 300 or 400 gun launches in the ports of Flanders, where I shall concentrate an army.
tweet: Your friendly letter is here — England arrogance is boundless. I mass 300 gunboats in Flanders with an army, another in Brittany for Brest. Naples and Sicily shut to the English; Bordeaux presses Portugal. Stop the northern trade with me.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Dispatch a night courier to General Murat, reaching Foligno tomorrow. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Night courier to Murat at Foligno: Rome instructions. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie d'expédier dans la nuit un courrier au général Murat, qui arrive demain à Foligno.
tweet: I dispatch a night courier to General Murat, reaching foligno tomorrow. The urgent orders ride through the night.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “But on the condition of the Spaniards giving us three of the frigates at Barcelona or Carthagena, and six of the line of battle ships at the Havannah. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: But on the condition of the Spaniards giving us three of the frigates at Barcelona or Carthagena, and six of the line of battle ships at the Havannah.
tweet: Madrid must show ten ships within the month — to catch English squadrons in the Straits or join our Mediterranean force. I demand our six vessels, Lucca for Parma against Tuscany, Havana frigates — and a Portuguese province as surety.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send Madrid the great interest I take in Spain's navy acting again. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Spain must make its navy act: recapitulatory dispatch. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Expédiez un courrier à l'ambassadeur à Madrid; vous lui récapitulerez le grand intérêt que j'attache à voir les Espagnols reprendre de l'activité.
tweet: Send Madrid the great interest I take in Spain's navy acting again. The Spanish fleet must return to the seas.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Brigade Chief Savary rides post-haste to Lorient. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Savary rides post-haste to Lorient for the Anacreon. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le chef de brigade Savary partira en toute diligence pour se rendre à Lorient.
tweet: I Brigade Chief Savary rides post-haste to lorient. The trusted aide carries urgent orders.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “BONAPARTE." Maury, of lamp-post fame, the inventor of the appellation sans culottes was at that moment acting as agent for Louis XVIII. at the Papal Court. He soon afterwards became the devoted adherent of Bonaparte, and remained devoted until 18 14. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Eleven months of peace — and Josephine's summers. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Maury welcomed: Louis's agent turned adherent.
tweet: Write Rome: I regret the honors paid to Cardinal Maury and condemn the prelate conduct.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order Brigadier-General Houdetot to start immediately for Rochefort. Give the same order to two or three officers who can fix public attention on the proposed expedition […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To Forfait: Order Brigadier-General Houdetot to start immediately for Rochefort.
tweet: I want Houdetot at Rochefort at once, with two or three officers to draw all eyes to the expedition.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “He was not then aware that the maritime confederation had experienced two fatal blows, and that the Russian alliance was at an end, owing to the death of Paul, and Nelson's victory in the Baltic. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Eleven months of peace — and Josephine's summers. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Madrid offers ships: three vessels plus a fifty-gunner.
tweet: Good news from Madrid: three Cadiz vessels, a fifty-gun ship and two Carthagena frigates for me.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The English when in dread of an invasion had carriages constructed capable of transporting twenty-two men, which, drawn by four horses, conveyed them rapidly from one point to another. " Circumstances constantly occur when similar carriages might be employed with advantage. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To his chief of staff Berthier: The English when in dread of an invasion had carriages constructed capable of transporting twenty-two men, which, drawn by four horses…
tweet: I want one of those English invasion carriages built for trial — twenty-two men, four horses, fast between points. If it answers, build more.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will let him know that after having presented it he must endeavour to have Dutheil and Georges arrested, or at least sent to America, should objections be raised to handing them over to the French Government. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: You will let him know that after having presented it he must endeavour to have Dutheil and Georges arrested, or at least sent to America…
voice: @talleyrand You will let him know that after having presented it he must endeavour to have Dutheil and Georges arrested, or at least sent to America…
tweet: Forward my note to Citizen Otto: have Dutheil and Georges arrested, or shipped to America if London objects to handing them over.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Consuls regret considerable differences in military accountants' books. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Military accountants differ considerably: report. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Les Consuls voient avec peine qu'il existe des différences considérables dans les comptes des divisions militaires.
tweet: I the Consuls regret considerable differences in military accountants' books. The financial accounts must be reconciled.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The grief I experience at the death of a prince I held in such great esteem prevents me from entering into details. His eldest son, who has succeeded him, has received the oath of the army and of the capital. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his brother Joseph: The grief I experience at the death of a prince I held in such great esteem prevents me from entering into details.
voice: The grief I experience at the death of a prince I held in such great esteem prevents me from entering into details
tweet: The Emperor of Russia died of apoplexy, and I grieve a prince I esteemed too much for details. His eldest son has the army and the capital oath.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will get presented to the Empress and you will take care to speak to her of my esteem and attachment for her family, and that of the Margrave of Baden. Both at Berlin and St. Petersburg you will speak as if we are sure of being able to hold Egypt. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his palace marshal Duroc: You will get presented to the Empress and you will take care to speak to her of my esteem and attachment for her family, and that of the Margrave of Baden.
voice: @duroc You will get presented to the Empress and you will take care to speak to her of my esteem and attachment for her family, and that of the Margrave of Baden
tweet: You start in Floréal for Petersburg by Berlin — two days there. Congratulate the king on Hanover for me, press my esteem on the Empress and Baden Margrave, and everywhere speak as if Egypt holds.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “He will be at Florence in forty days, and I desire you will remain there in order to instal him. I await with impatience the news of the occupation of the isle of Elba. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Eleven months of peace — and Josephine's summers. To his brother-in-law Murat: Murat to hold Florence; Elba eyed.
voice: I await with impatience the news of the occupation of the isle of Elba
tweet: The king of Tuscany leaves Madrid for Paris, Florence in forty days — stay and instal him. I hunger for Elba news. Tell me: is Abbé Bonaparte of San-Miniato alive?

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That the feelings of Alexander I. and his cabinet are ill known in London if it be supposed he will ever betray the cause of the continental Powers; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To his foreign minister Talleyrand: That the feelings of Alexander I. and his cabinet are ill known in London if it be supposed he will ever betray the cause of the continental Powers.
tweet: Tell Otto to laugh Hawkesbury anecdotes away: my cabinet is one, and wants only an honourable peace on balanced seas. France is not intimidated — and London mistakes Alexander if it thinks he betrays the continent.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Several of Georges's band wish to submit. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Georges's band seeks submission: hear them. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Plusieurs individus de la bande de Georges témoignent le désir de se soumettre.
tweet: I several of georges's band wish to submit. The chouan rebels seek amnesty.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The war minister gathers battalions at Brest. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Battalions to Brest: 30th light, 31st, 71st, 77th, 79th. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le ministre de la guerre donnera les ordres pour réunir à Brest un bataillon de la 30e légère, un de la 31e, un de la 71e.
tweet: I the War minister gathers battalions at Brest. The port prepares for the expedition.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The prefects in the departmients, owing to over zeal, have exceeded the honours to be paid to the Count and Countess of Leghorn. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Eleven months of peace — and Josephine's summers. To his interior minister Chaptal: Prefects scolded over Leghorn honours.
tweet: The prefects honored the count and Countess of Leghorn beyond measure. Tell the Seine prefect for me: no civil authority visits them.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The commissary -general of police at Bordeaux was stupid enough to allow couplets to be sung in honour of the King of Tuscany. As he is called Louis this gave rise to ill-natured allusions. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his police minister Fouché: The commissary-general of police at Bordeaux was stupid enough to allow couplets to be sung in honour of the King of Tuscany.
tweet: Your Bordeaux commissary let couplets for the Tuscan king — called Louis! — invite sedition. See that no verse is read or sung in any theatre or square.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Honoured custom. It will be proper for the Batavian, Helvetic, Ligurian, and Cisalpine Republics to recognise the new monarch. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Honoured custom. It will be proper for the Batavian, Helvetic, Ligurian, and Cisalpine Republics to recognise the new monarch.
tweet: It is my will that Madrid man at Rome send a legate to Florence complimenting Etruria king — custom demands it.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They are nursed by convicts. Would it not be possible to establish Sisters of Charity at Toulon as at Brest? […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To Forfait: The sick are not well cared for at Toulon.
tweet: Toulon sick lie neglected, officers absent, convicts nursing. Put Sisters of Charity there as at Brest — I will have it so.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see with pleasure that you are ready to sail. Your arrival in the Mediterranean is all the more important because the English are preparing to reinforce their army at Aboukir. […]”
sourceTitle: To Admiral Bruix, Prairial 1801 (revolutionary date; day approximate)
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Prairial Year IX: ready to sail. Revolutionary calendar date; rendered to the 1st, marked approximate.
tweet: I see with pleasure that you are ready to sail. Your arrival in the Mediterranean is all the more important because the English are preparing to reinforce their army at Aboukir. The fleet must contest the Eastern Mediterranean.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Notify by express that Moncey commands French troops in Cisalpine. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Moncey commands French troops in Cisalpine: notify by express. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Faites connaître par un courrier extraordinaire que le général Moncey est nommé commandant des troupes françaises dans la Cisalpine.
tweet: I notify by express that moncey commands French troops in Cisalpine. The command appointment is announced at speed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Cyr. Under these circumstances the King of Portugal agreed to close his ports to England, to cede Olivenza to Spain, and to pay France 20,000,000 francs. This treaty was signed by Lucien Bonaparte, who was heavily bribed by the two contracting parties. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Cyr. Under these circumstances the King of Portugal agreed to close his ports to England, to cede Olivenza to Spain, and to pay France 20,000,000 francs.
tweet: Disown this magnificent treaty by extraordinary courier — it breaks its instructions, our Spanish treaty, our interests, and favors England. Occupy three provinces or keep the colonies; I call it one of my worst reverses.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tell him: 'doge' and 'podestat' suit Liguria better. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Doge and podestat beat other titles for Liguria. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Faites-lui connaître: 1° Que les mots doge, podestat sont meilleurs que les autres titres proposés.
tweet: I tell him: 'doge' and 'podestat' suit liguria better. The ligurian constitution reflects its own traditions.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tell Murat the frigates Bravoure, Carrère, Succès reached Livorno for cruising. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Bravoure, Carrère, Succès frigates to cruise from Livorno. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Faites connaître au général Murat que les frégates la Bravoure, la Carrère et le Succès doivent être arrivées à Livourne.
tweet: I Tell Murat the frigates bravoure, carriere, succes reached livorno for cruising. The squadron is on station.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “When the legislative ORDERS TO EMBARK FOR ENGLAND, 1 37 body has finished its sittings, retire for a month to Monza, and have the palace at Milan fitted up. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To his stepson Eugène: When the legislative ORDERS TO EMBARK FOR ENGLAND, 1 37 body has finished its sittings, retire for a month to Monza, and have the palace at Milan fitted up.
tweet: Eighty-five hours from Turin, delayed by mountains and the Empress breakfasts. When the legislature rises, retire to Monza and fit Milan palace — I want a straight walk through the state rooms to the Place du Dôme side.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Since you have not been to Naples I see no objection to your going there after you have arranged matters in Tuscany. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his brother-in-law Murat: Since you have not been to Naples I see no objection to your going there after you have arranged matters in Tuscany.
tweet: Your letter is here. Troops watch the Adriatic against Turks and English; Naples is yours once Tuscany settles. Pick up local knowledge — examine Capua and the forts, return by Ancona.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Cardinal Consalvi will inform you of my desire to do all in my power to contribute to your happiness. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To Pope Pius VII: Cardinal Consalvi will inform you of my desire to do all in my power to contribute to your happiness.
voice: @pope Cardinal Consalvi will inform you of my desire to do all in my power to contribute to your happiness
tweet: Consalvi gave me your letter — I recognize the Gospel in it. You shall have my support while you preach peace; but Europe tears I cannot dry. Count always on your devoted son.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tell journalists, political and literary, to abstain from all religious matter. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Journalists forbidden to touch religion. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Faites connaître aux journalistes, tant politiques que littéraires, qu'ils doivent s'abstenir de parler de tout ce qui peut concerner la religion.
tweet: I tell journalists, political and literary, to abstain from all religious matter. The Press must not inflame theological disputes.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send Levavasseur post to Brest to inspect coast batteries. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Levavasseur to Brest: extraordinary coast-battery inspection. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de donner l'ordre au général Levavasseur de se rendre en poste à Brest pour l'inspection des batteries de côtes.
tweet: I send levavasseur post to Brest to inspect coast batteries. The coastal defences are inspected.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will inform the prefects that the despatch of these citizens should be made without noise, and that the object of this measure is to arrange means for maintaining order, liberty, and independence of worship. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his interior minister Chaptal: You will inform the prefects that the despatch of these citizens should be made without noise…
voice: @chaptal You will inform the prefects that the despatch of these citizens should be made without noise, and that the object of this measure is to arrange means for maintaining order, liberty…
tweet: Order the five departments prefects and Geneva: send me each one leading Protestant minister — no fanatics, only upright, sensible, esteemed men — quietly, to settle order, liberty and worship.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Redo the Year X army organisation at unchanged pay. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Redo the Year X organisation keeping all pay rates. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de me refaire l'organisation de l'armée pour l'an X, en laissant partout les mêmes appointements.
tweet: I redo the yEAR x army organisation at unchanged pay. The army structure is reformed without cutting soldiers' pay.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I read the committee's observations; nothing reasonable in them. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Committee observations unreasonable; draft near the mark. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai lu les observations du comité; il n'y a rien de raisonnable.
tweet: I read the committee's observations; nothing reasonable in them. The Consul dismisses the committee's critique.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Let Citizen Cibou also know that I take an interest in Hompesch, and that I shall see him with great pleasure resume his functions of Grand Master; as I know he is in distress, authorise Citizen Cacault to give him 500 louis, without a letter or anything ostensible. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

tweet: Sound Vienna and Rome on Hompesch through Champagny and Cacault — off-hand, our support if they back him. Tell Cibou I take interest in the man and want him restored as Grand Master; 500 louis secretly, he is in need.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: Answer Otto: no Tobago. Demerara and Portugal stand settled. Time presses with the equinox — I negotiate with all Europe and will give no color of bad faith; the squadrons stay till preliminaries sign.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: Send the War minister our Batavian convention: we keep Flushing, and our Batavia commander gets secret orders to match.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It should agree with the usages and with the civil cut of VOL. I. B B the consular costume, and be designed to receive for ornament the Regent and other diamonds of great price. […]”

context: Paris. To his interior minister Chaptal: B B the consular costume, and be designed to receive for ornament the Regent and other diamonds of great price.
tweet: Have me a sabre model — moderate, handy, consular cut, set for the Regent and the great diamonds. I want it for Brumaire anniversary and the peace feast.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: I have the salines' receipts. Warn the farmers the government watches. The salt monopoly is enforced.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: I have a handy medium saber modelled. The cavalry weapon is standardised.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: The peace with England, Portugal, Russia, and the Ottoman Porte having been signed, I hasten to inform your Holiness of this fact, knowing the interest you take in the happiness and tranquillity of nations.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Domingo. *-" It will be necessary to inform the court of Spain that it is essential for it to send some one with full powers to Amiens, the English and ourselves being determined to arrange natters promptly […]”

tweet: Tell Hawkesbury through Otto: Rochefort and part of Brest sail with 12,000 men to restore St. Domingo. Spain must send plenipotentiaries to Amiens — haste, for England and I will arrange promptly.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will send passports to the persons concerned, and when they arrive in Paris you will hand them the decrees, but only after they have sworn fidelity to the Republic and have renounced all foreign […]”

context: Paris. To his police minister Fouché: You will send passports to the persons concerned, and when they arrive in Paris you will hand them the decrees…

tweet: I have signed fourteen radiations — passport the men, hand the decrees in Paris only after they swear the Republic and renounce everything foreign.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Saint-Domingue's people, whatever origin or color, are all Frenchmen, all free, all equal before God and Republic. […]”

tweet: I saint-domingue's people, whatever origin or color, are all Frenchmen, all free, all equal before God and Republic. Liberty, equality, fraternity for all.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Frenchmen, yours at last entire, this peace earned by such long generous efforts! […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)

originalText: Français, vous l'avez enfin tout entière cette paix que vous avez méritée par de si longs et si généreux efforts!
tweet: Frenchmen, yours at last entire, this peace earned by such long generous efforts! The Amiens peace is won by your sacrifices.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

originalText: Vous ferez connaître au général Montchoisy que le Gouvernement ne reconnaît point le Gouvernement helvétique.
tweet: I tell montchoisy Paris disowns the Helvetic government. The Swiss puppet regime has no French backing.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

originalText: Le citoyen Sage fait connaître la situation malheureuse de Volta, professeur à Pavie, maintenant à Paris.
tweet: I citizen sage reports volta's hard case at Paris. The scientist's situation is reviewed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That peace will therefore be promptly signed whether Spain participates in it or not; […]”

context: Paris. To Hauterive: That peace will therefore be promptly signed whether Spain participates in it or not.
tweet: Tell Azara Amiens closes — Spain delayed us six weeks, and France with England cannot lose a day. We sign with or without her. Out of kindness for Charles, my intimate ally, I sign his name myself rather than shame him.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They were ignorant of the peace Three vessels and four frigates, with 3,000 infantry are about to sail in order to disarm the blacks and to restore tranquillity. […]”

context: Paris. To his brother Joseph: I am about to start for Lyons. … I believe that General Bernadotte [Joseph's brother-in-law] is at Amiens.
tweet: I leave for Lyons. Bernadotte may take Guadeloupe — prosperous, cultivated, though Lacrosse offended them and 500 whites fled a mulatto chief. Three vessels, four frigates, 3,000 men sail to disarm and pacify — an agreeable mission.

tweet: All the Eastern officers I meet confirm the reports against several generals.

tweet: I hasten to Tell Your Holiness the Cisalpine Republic's affairs are arranged. The Italian Sister Republic is settled.

tweet: General Silly reports Your Majesty's welcome to 300 French forced by sea onto Sicily. The Neapolitan king shows hospitality to our castaways.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: Your 12 Pluviose letter received. All moves at Amiens. Eight days more or less are now indifferent. The peace negotiations proceed at their own pace.

tweet: I Article 1: memoirs, plans, drawings, all science and arts results of the Egypt expedition, shall be published at government expense. The Egyptian legacy is preserved for posterity.

tweet: Glad to read you firmly constituted. You are a small state; live tranquil; shun faction. Lucca's independence depends on unity.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: Five in the evening, no courier yet. Otto and all England letters confirm great armaments and sailing squadrons; Cornwallis has his last orders. Report to me twice daily, morning and evening — without peace signed, London must change system.

tweet: France rejoices at your opening — Toulon, Cadiz, Flushing and Havre squadrons should have joined you. Follow your instructions to the letter: rid me of Toussaint, Christophe, Dessalines and the brigand chiefs, disarm the masses, ship the coloured fighters to the Continent.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

voice: @talleyrand You will perceive how I look upon the question
tweet: The Valais must be settled — you see my view. Get me a memorandum on its ancient organisation. Helvetia, no French province, governs itself; the Valais is my affair. Warn Reding: refuse my middle way and lose everything.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

tweet: Enclosed, my Amiens treaty — Etruria and the sister republics untouched for now, to be recognized shortly. Both sides know this peace is a truce.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They will take the oath, in presence of the First Consul, on Easter-day." The archbishops were to receive 15,000, and the bishops 10,000 francs each for preliminary expenses, but this matter was to be kept secret. […]”

tweet: The nominations stand, though I cannot yet deliver the brevets. Settle with the Legate: consecrations and institutions at once, Easter oath before me. Archbishops 15,000, bishops 10,000 — in strict secret.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Most Holy Father-I have left it to Cardinal Caprara to inform you of all that happened on Easter Day. You would have been greatly affected at the splendid spectacle offered by the entire Republic upon that occasion. […]”

voice: @pope You would have been greatly affected at the splendid spectacle offered by the entire Republic upon that occasion
tweet: Caprara will tell you our Easter — all the Republic in splendor that moved even you. Murat warns some constitutional bishops trouble you; I named ex-bishops too, for schisms end only by reunion. Rejoice — all France holds the Concordat.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is indispensable for you to inform Citizen Alquier that the King of Naples must allow the Pope to enjoy the integrity of his States, and that Beneventum and Ponte Corvo should be placed on their ancient footing. […]”

tweet: I insist Alquier hear it plainly: Naples must respect the Pope states entire — Beneventum and Ponte Corvo back on their ancient footing.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Take measures to prevent any vessel, no matter to what nation it belongs, being blockaded or captured in our waters”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

voice: Take measures to prevent any vessel, no matter to what nation it belongs, being blockaded or captured in our waters
tweet: A Barbary ship has been blockading a dozen Ligurian vessels at St. Tropez, and the Maritime Prefect has done nothing to disengage the port. It is a dishonour to the Republic that these Barbary wretches should insult our Coasts.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That unless he behaves well I shall punish him as I did the Mamelukes." And the consul was to be instructed to speak imperiously to the Dey, and not to fear bringing about a rupture. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

tweet: Write my man at Algiers: demand the reis head for bastinadoing our captain and restore the ship. Warn the Dey — listeners to France enemies are ruined; none insults me unpunished. Speak imperiously, rupture or not.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Bonaparte threatened the Dey with an army of 80,000 men, and the Dey threatened the First Consul with the horrors of war unless he were paid his 200,000 piastres, and there the matter stopped. To CITIZEN ABRIAL, Minister of Justice, Paris, 21st August, 1802. […]”

context: Eleven months of peace — and Josephine's summers. To The Dey Of Algiers: Threatened the Dey with an army of 80,000 men, and the Dey threatened the First Consul with the horrors of war unless he were paid his 200,000 piastres…
tweet: Magnificent Dey — my adjutant demands reparation for insults to my flag, and your 200,000 piastres demand disgusts me. I never paid anyone; thank God, I lay the law on all my enemies. I crushed the Mamelukes for demanding money after insulting my flag.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Most Holy Father, — I have read the letter of your Holiness with the greatest attention. / can but approve of the. […]”

voice: @pope Most Holy Father, — I have read the letter of your Holiness with the greatest attention
tweet: I have read your letter with full attention. I approve your naming one of my subjects Grand Master of Malta. It pains me you see no Concordat with Italy — consider my cardinals: Paris, Lyons, Troyes, Autun. Old Paris is sound at ninety-three; young Lyons shows promise.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Archbishop of Turin, having asked to be dispensed from coming to Paris owing to his great age, his ill-health, the requirements of his diocese, and want of means”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Eleven months of peace — and Josephine's summers. To Portalis: The Archbishop of Turin, having asked to be dispensed from coming to Paris owing to his great age, his ill-health, the requirements of his diocese, and want of means.
tweet: I send you a note forwarded by the Inspector general of Gendarmery concerning the Bishop of Rennes.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We shall take our revenge to-morrow, which is All Saints' Day. The Grand Judge should not lose a moment in having the notary Petit arrested and confined in the Temple. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

voice: We shall take our revenge to-morrow, which is All Saints' Day
tweet: I rode Rouen heights at 8 — the beloved Archbishop said mass but no Holy water, no prayer for me. We take revenge tomorrow, all Saints day. Notary Petit to the Temple at once; the eight curés under guard to Italy.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “All that I have read of your work appears to me perfectly clear. I long to be able to devote a few weeks to finish reading it, and I much regret not being able to give it the time and attention it deserves. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Eleven months of peace — and Josephine's summers. To the savant Laplace: All that I have read of your work appears to me perfectly clear.

tweet: All I have read of your work strikes me as perfectly clear. I long to give it weeks of study, and I rue the press of affairs that steals me from the sciences. I accept your dedication gladly; let posterity remember my esteem and friendship for its author.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “However, desiring to be agreeable to your Majesty, I did not press for the execution of the treaty. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Spain, St. Cloud, 1802-11-27

context: Eleven months of peace — and Josephine's summers. To the Spanish king: However, desiring to be agreeable to your Majesty, I did not press for the execution of the treaty.
tweet: Your letter is here — condolences on Parma. France had the right to take your states two years ago, yet I forbore for love of you. But I cannot break my own signed treaty; Europe would cry shame to see Ferdinand stripped and Sardinia king waiting.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Piedmont's church affairs need settling. If France has a bishop per two departments, six may stay in Piedmont. […]”

tweet: I Piedmont's church affairs need settling. If France has a Bishop per two departments, six may stay in Piedmont. The ecclesiastical map is redrawn.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Report on wood-cutting bills as paper money. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)

originalText: Le Premier Consul désire que vous fassiez un rapport sur les traites de coupes de bois à organiser comme papier-monnaie.
tweet: I report on wood-cutting bills as paper money. The forest revenue is audited.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Only germinal/messidor wood payments fund Year XI; the rest Year XII. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Wood revenues split Year XI/XII by month of falling due. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Mon intention est de n'affecter au service de l'an XI, sur la coupe des bois, que les payements qui échoient en germinal et en messidor.
tweet: I direct only Germinal and Messidor timber receipts to fund Year XI; the rest to Year XII.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tell General Brune to demand instant restitution of Citizen Ruffin's ship, seized by Djezzar-Pasha. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Deputies, your fatherland is critical. Moderation, prudence, sacrificed passions alone can save it. […]”

tweet: Deputies, your fatherland is critical. Moderation, prudence, sacrificed passions alone can save it. Switzerland's survival depends on restraint.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order plans for Quiberon, Belle-Île and Boulogne batteries. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Plans for Quiberon, Belle-Île, Marcouf, Boulogne works. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de donner ordre de dresser des plans pour mettre le fort Quiberon, la place de Belle-Île et les batteries de Boulogne en état.
tweet: I order plans for Quiberon, belle-ile and Boulogne batteries. The coastal defences are planned.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They are the tyrants of India; they are suspicious and jealous; the Captain-General must act with gentleness, dissimulation, and simplicity. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: To his navy minister Decrès: The Captain-General (of East Indian possessions) will arrive in a country where our rivals dominate.
tweet: The new Captain-General reaches an India ruled by rivals — give them no alarm. Confine yourself to indispensable business, and within six months send me the full picture: peoples, princes, and their temper under the English yoke.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Read the enclosed report. 'Liquidation of newly created pensions' means nothing to me. […]”
