originalText: Je vous prie de prendre connaissance du rapport ci-joint. Je ne conçois pas ce que veut dire ce mot de liquidation des pensions nouvellement créées.
tweet: Read the enclosed report. 'Liquidation of newly created pensions' means nothing to me. The pension accounts are opaque.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The 1,200 sailed from Havre, Dunkerque ready, three Toulon expeditions: troops arriving together. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Glad of Fort Dauphin retaken; take directly my full confidence and approval of vigorous measures. […]”

context: Fort Dauphin retaken with pleasure: full confidence, vigorous measures approved. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.

tweet: Glad of Fort Dauphin retaken; take directly my full confidence and approval of vigorous measures. Rochambeau earns my trust.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Fifteen thousand men shipped or shipping to Saint-Domingue. Combine now a 6,500 expedition. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)

originalText: Quinze mille hommes viennent ou vont finir d'être expédiés à Saint-Domingue. Mais il faut combiner, dès aujourd'hui, une expédition de 6,500 hommes.
tweet: I fifteen thousand men shipped or shipping to saint-domingue. Combine now a 6,500 expedition. The colony receives massive reinforcements.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order the Brisgau commander to receive two Austrian companies. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Two Austrian companies into Brisgau: no obstacle. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie d'ordonner au commandant dans le Brisgau de recevoir deux compagnies de troupes autrichiennes.
tweet: I order the brisgau commander to receive two Austrian companies. The border garrison accepts the enemy detachment.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My trust in your great talents bids me ask an elementary mathematics work for the national lycées. […]”

originalText: La confiance que j'ai dans vos grands talents me porte à désirer que vous vous chargiez de faire un ouvrage élémentaire pour la classe de mathématiques des Lycées nationaux.
tweet: My trust in your great talents bids me ask an elementary mathematics work for the national lycees. Haüy, write the textbook for the new schools.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The nègre Télémaque thanks the First Consul for the Cap mayoralty, protesting devotion to the Republic. […]”

context: Black mayor thanks and devotion: recommend this brave nègre. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le nègre Télémaque remercie le Premier Consul de l'avoir nommé maire du Cap. Il proteste de son dévouement à la République.
tweet: I the negre telemague thanks the first Consul for the cap mayoralty, protesting devotion to the Republic. The black mayor pledges loyalty.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Madame de Staël, forbidden Paris, reaches Melun the 20th. Order police to turn her straight back. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Staël forbidden Paris, arrives at Melun: turn her back at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je suis instruit que madame de Staël, malgré la défense qui lui a été faite de venir à Paris, arrive le 20 à Melun. Donnez ordre de la faire sur-le-champ rétrograder.
tweet: I Madame de staël, forbidden Paris, reaches melun the. Order police to turn her straight back. The exile is enforced at the gates.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “7 Constantine, tell him that I regret he did not come to Paris. You will speak to the Empress of the pleasure I experienced on seeing her uncle here, and how he amused himself in Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

voice: @colbert You will speak to the Empress of the pleasure I experienced on seeing her uncle here, and how he amused himself in Paris
tweet: You go to Russia with my letter. Speak of how Paris esteems Russians, talk philosophy not trifles with the Emperor. If Constantine appears, tell him I regret he missed Paris. If England comes up, say France longs to measure swords with her.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “BONAPARTE." You will know much better than I can tell you how this emigrant duke has been courted by Buonaparte, through his minister in Russia. We must recollect that he is a Frenchman, and his ultimate views probably turn to getting back some of his estates in France. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

voice: @berthier You will know much better than I can tell you how this emigrant duke has been courted by Buonaparte, through his minister in Russia
tweet: I Order Monnet to Flushing with full authority, no Dutch interference — the place is Franco-Dutch common ground, and everything goes in France name. Treat their People and officers well, and talk to them often.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter reached me at the Malmaison. I desire that the conference should not degenerate into a conversation. Show yourself cold, haughty, and even somewhat proud. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Amiens ruptured: the truce is over, the invasion army rises.
tweet: Your letter reached me at the Malmaison. I desire that the conference should not degenerate into a conversation. Show yourself cold, haughty, and even somewhat proud.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “If the note does not contain this word, make him insert it, remarking that we must really know whereabout we are, and that we are weary of this state of uncertainty. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: If the note does not contain this word, make him insert it, remarking that we must really know whereabout we are, and that we are weary of this state of uncertainty.
tweet: Your Malmaison letter is here. Be cold, haughty, even proud with Whitworth: if his note says ultimatum, tell him that word means war, and that superiors do not negotiate with inferiors so. If it lacks the word, make him insert it — we must know where we stand.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received the different letters which it has pleased your majesty to write to me. Circumstances become more and more serious, and war is about to be rekindled between France and England. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Prince Regent Of Portugal, St.  Cloud, 1803-05-10
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

voice: @regent I have received the different letters which it has pleased your majesty to write to me
tweet: Your letters please me, but war with England rekindles and I have done all to spare the world. Unite every Power for Malta independence — I count on the sentiments you have expressed.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “25,000 francs to M. Chatillon; 30,000 to the Bishop of Orleans, and 25,000 to the Prefect of the Loire-Inferieure. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

tweet: I beg you will hand 100,000 francs to Colonel Sebastiani for secret expenses; 25,000 francs to M. Chatillon; 30,000 to the Bishop of Orleans, and 25,000 to the Prefect of the Loire-Inferieure.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have directed this general to make the army defile with the honours of war, to disarm it, to dismount the cavalry, and to send it prisoner to France. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: I have directed this general to make the army defile with the honours of war, to disarm it, to dismount the cavalry, and to send it prisoner to France.
voice: I have directed this general to make the army defile with the honours of war, to disarm it, to dismount the cavalry, and to send it prisoner to France
tweet: My orders go to Mortier for the Hanover army: England refused the Prairial convention, so capitulate — defile with honours, disarm, dismount, march prisoner to France. Warn Laforest in Berlin first, for his troops must move within days of the order.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter, good little Josephine. I perceived with sorrow that you suffered from the journey. But a few days of repose will do much for you, I am very well, indeed. I went yesterday to the hunt at Marly,1 and wounded myself very slightly in one finger, in shooting a boar. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Malmaison summer: health anxieties.
tweet: I have received your letter, good little Josephine. I perceived with sorrow that you suffered from the journey. But a few days of repose will do much for you. I am very well.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I recommend you to be inflexible as regards its execution, and not to permit the introduction of any English goods or couriers. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To General Mortier: I recommend you to be inflexible as regards its execution, and not to permit the introduction of any English goods or couriers.
voice: @mortier I recommend you to be inflexible as regards its execution, and not to permit the introduction of any English goods or couriers
tweet: I approve your Hanover Convention. Be inflexible — no English goods or couriers through. It will ruin English houses. Send me heavy cavalry horses, and disarm the country.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 29th of June. You do not speak of your health, or of the effect of the baths. I see that you intend to be on your return in eight days. That will afford great pleasure to your friend, who wearies of being alone. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Her letter answered; health unwritten.
tweet: I have received your letter of the of. You do not speak of your health, or of the effect of the baths. I see that you intend to be on your return in eight days. That will afford great pleasure to your Friend, who wearies of being alone.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The affairs of Ireland make me' feel the necessity of your having some private conferences with the chiefs of the United Irishmen now in Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Flotilla orders: flatboats, tides, Boulogne.
tweet: Irish affairs move me to order secret talks with the United Irish chiefs in Paris. Offer them twenty-five thousand men, forty thousand muskets, guns and powder, and pledge no peace with England till Ireland stands free, if twenty thousand join us on landing.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I shall arrive at St. Cloud when least expected, perhaps during the night. The next day I shall receive the authorities. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To Consul Cambacirils: I shall arrive at St. Cloud when least expected, perhaps during the night.
voice: I shall arrive at St. Cloud when least expected, perhaps during the night
tweet: I shall reach St. Cloud unannounced, perhaps by night, and receive the authorities next day. I feel the Tribunate good will all the same.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You can offer them 25,000 men, 40,000 muskets, with artillery and ammunition, and assure them that the Government will undertake not to make peace with England until the independence of Ii-eland has been proclaimed; provided that 20,000 United Irishmen join the French army on its landing. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his navy minister Decrès: You can offer them 25,000 men, 40,000 muskets, with artillery and ammunition, and assure them that the Government will undertake not to make peace with England until the…

tweet: The Irish chiefs in Paris need secret talks — offer 25,000 men, 40,000 muskets with guns and powder, and my pledge of no separate peace with England before a free Ireland is proclaimed. Twenty thousand of them with our landing force.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The most important matter with regard to our relations with Spain is not the question of subsidies; it is not the execution of the treaty by which we are bound, but it is — 1st, The strange conduct of having allowed two vessels anchored at Algesiras to be cut out, and not offering an indemnity. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: The most important matter with regard to our relations with Spain is not the question of subsidies.
voice: The most important matter with regard to our relations with Spain is not the question of subsidies
tweet: Spain matters more than subsidies or treaties to me: two of our ships cut out at Algeciras without redress; four warships left bare at Corunna before the enemy like Barbary prizes; 100,000 militia raised, plainly not for British fleets.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think it will be useful to send the last note from Russia to Laforest. He can communicate it to M. de Haugwitz, pointing out all its absurdity. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: I think it will be useful to send the last note from Russia to Laforest.
voice: I think it will be useful to send the last note from Russia to Laforest
tweet: Send Laforest Russia latest note to show Haugwitz its absurdity. England gets from me only Amiens — nothing in the Mediterranean. I evacuate Holland and Switzerland; Otranto, Tarentum and Hanover go when Malta does.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I return you the despatch from Madrid of the 13th Fructidor. I am surprised that we have no other news. Make out a list of all the complaints we have against Spain, so that we may have materials ready in the event of requiring them.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Invasion diplomacy between reviews.
tweet: I return you the despatch from Madrid of the Fructidor. I am surprised that we have no other news. Make out a list of all the complaints we have against Spain, so that we may have materials ready in the event of requiring them.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “And if so, whether in the event of their coming to Syria or Egypt they will be secured from pillage and looked upon as friends. Our agent must endeavour to procure information with regard to the force and situation of this new sect. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: And if so, whether in the event of their coming to Syria or Egypt they will be secured from pillage and looked upon as friends.
voice: Our agent must endeavour to procure information with regard to the force and situation of this new sect
tweet: Write our Aleppo agent: does the Wahhabi chief protect Frenchmen crossing his lands to Syria and Egypt from pillage as friends? Get me his force and position. And tell Rousseau to open Persia and write oftener; send Brune to learn who commands at Constantinople.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “If this be the case I beg you will withdraw it, for the troops will fall ill. Should the English attempt an attack on the Isle of Walcheren you will have time to succour it. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To Marshal Davout: Should the English attempt an attack on the Isle of Walcheren you will have time to succour it.
voice: @davout Should the English attempt an attack on the Isle of Walcheren you will have time to succour it
tweet: Withdraw that Cadzand demi-brigade — the men will sicken. If England tries Walcheren there is time. Health first: sickly quarters melt armies to nothing, and Walcheren already costs us dear.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am informed. Citizen Minister, that Madame de Stael has arrived at Maffiers. Let her be informed through one of her friends, without making a scandal, that if on the 8th she has not taken her departure she shall be escorted to the frontier by the gendarmery. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his grand-judge Régnier: I am informed. Citizen Minister, that Madame de Stael has arrived at Maffiers.
tweet: I am informed. Citizen minister, that Madame de Stael has arrived at Maffiers. Let her be informed through one of her friends, without making a scandal, that if she still lingers, the gendarmes escort her to the frontier.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is not my intention no matter what the pretext, to allow this ridiculous pretension to exist. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: It is not my intention no matter what the pretext, to allow this ridiculous pretension to exist.
tweet: I was shocked to hear the Spanish ambassador dispute precedence with France minister at Florence. Tell me if Clarke has written — I will not suffer this ridiculous pretension on any pretext.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is time for you to propose the formation of the Irish battalions. I wish you to hand me a return of the Irish who are here, and who count upon joining the expedition, to settle their rank, &c. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his chief of staff Berthier: It is time for you to propose the formation of the Irish battalions.
voice: @berthier I wish you to hand me a return of the Irish who are here, and who count upon joining the expedition, to settle their rank, &c
tweet: It is time you proposed the Irish battalions. Hand me a roll of the Irish here counting on the expedition, to settle rank and business.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have ordered them to be settled, my intention being, under no circumstances, to borrow money from the bank. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To Perregaux: I have ordered them to be settled, my intention being, under no circumstances, to borrow money from the bank.
tweet: I understand your note perfectly. Settle the pending Bank-Treasury transactions — but never borrow from the Bank on any account. Tell Lebrun to strengthen the Bank confidence; I will aid it always.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I know that several comedies appropriate to the circumstance have been presented. A choice should be made so that they may be played in the various theatres of Paris, and especially at the camps of Boulogne, Bruges, and other places where the army is quartered. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his interior minister Chaptal: I know that several comedies appropriate to the circumstance have been presented.
voice: I know that several comedies appropriate to the circumstance have been presented
tweet: I beg you will have a song written for the invasion of England to the Chant du départ tune — more songs, more tunes. Pick the comedies fit for Paris theatres and especially the Boulogne and Bruges camps where the army lies.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I return you your despatches, Citizen Minister. Tell Citizen Laforest that I have read his despatch with great interest. It will be well to warn the Turkish ambassador that the English, who evidently encourage the Beys, intend to seize upon Egypt.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: From the invasion camp.
tweet: I return you your despatches, Citizen minister. Tell Citizen Laforest that I have read his despatch with great interest. It will be well to warn the Turkish ambassador that the English, who evidently encourage the Beys, intend to seize upon Egypt.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Citizen General, — I have received your letter, and have given orders for hoods to be served out to all the men forming part of the expedition to Ireland, of which you shall have the command. Affairs are settled with Spain and Portugal. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Boulogne camps: invasion of England prepared.
tweet: Citizen general, I have received your letter, and have given orders for hoods to be served out to all the men forming part of the expedition to Ireland, of which you shall have the command. Affairs are settled with Spain and Portugal. Measures have been taken against desertion.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “He was made a senator in 1805, a count in 1809, a peer by the Bourbons in 1814, a commander of the Order of St. Louis in 18 16, a marshal the same year, and a marquis in 18 17. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To Augereau: Ireland expedition: Augereau commands.
tweet: Citizen general — I have your letter, and order hoods for every man of the Ireland expedition under you. Spain and Portugal are settled.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The solution of this problem offers such immense advantages that it is improbable anything reasonable can have been imagined by a Swiss mountaineer. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: The solution of this problem offers such immense advantages that it is improbable anything reasonable can have been imagined by a Swiss mountaineer.
tweet: Ney affair deserves no attention. But boats without men intrigue me — some Swiss mountaineer scheme promising wonders is hardly reasonable. Now Prussia: evacuation of Hanover? Preponderance in Germany?

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Let Madame Bourmont be examined as to the foreigner who paid her a visit a month ago. Let. her understand that the result of her examination may have important consequences, and that she ought to tell the truth clearly. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his grand-judge Régnier: Let Madame Bourmont be examined as to the foreigner who paid her a visit a month ago.
tweet: Put Madame Bourmont to the question for me about her foreign visitor of last month. Let her understand the examination matters, and tell the whole truth plainly.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received the letter in which you announce the arrival of forty sail in the Somme. I have also received the report of the visit made to the Prince de Galles. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To Admiral Bruix: I have also received the report of the visit made to the Prince de Galles.
voice: @bruix I have received the letter in which you announce the arrival of forty sail in the Somme
tweet: Your Somme letter is here, with the prince de Galles visit report. Fit her out as you propose for the guard sailors, with three more ships for my followers — and a howitzer aboard if she carries it easily.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That I know everything; that the brothers Bertin are paid by England, as is proved by the tone of their articles; that it is my intention to allow only those journals which excite the nation against England and encourage it to support the vicissitudes of war, to exist. […]”

tweet: I know everything: the Bertins Take English gold, proved by their articles tone. This is my last warning of displeasure — next they learn it by suppression. Only journals that rouse the nation against England and steel it for war will exist.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “De Coucy, the ex-Bishop of La Rochelle, is in Spain, where he is behaving very badly. His incendiary pastorals encourage the civil war in La Vendue. […]”

context: Flatboats, tides, and England watched. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: De Coucy, the ex-Bishop of La Rochelle, is in Spain, where he is behaving very badly.
tweet: Send Madrid an extraordinary courier: arrest Coucy and hand him to Bayonne gendarmes. His incendiary preachings shake the public peace, English-paid — I cannot believe His Catholic majesty will shield him. Tell Beurnonville: no empty formality.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I have not received any news from you for several days; I should, however, have been glad to know what effect the waters have had, and how you pass your time. I have been here for the last week, and intend going to-morrow to Boulogne. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

context: Paris. To his chief of staff Berthier: The message naturally contained the most terrible invectives against England.
tweet: Send for Emmet, Thomson, and the other Irish chiefs, and let them know that I have read the inclosed memorial with the greatest attention.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Citizen Tascher, officer of the Guard, you will start to-morrow for Rome. You will alight at the residence of Cardinal Fesch, Ambassador of the Republic, who will present you to the Pope, into whose hands you will deliver the inclosed letter. […]”

voice: @tascher You will alight at the residence of Cardinal Fesch, Ambassador of the Republic, who will present you to the Pope, into whose hands you will deliver the inclosed letter
tweet: Tascher, officer of my Guard — start tomorrow for Rome, lodge with Cardinal Fesch, and deliver my letter into the Pope hands. Stay till His Holiness answers, eight or ten days in the city.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Let him be sent to the first French posts at Rimini, and conveyed under escort to Paris. No attention should be paid to the steps taken by the Russians, because they have not been approved of by the Emperor. […]”

context: Paris. To his uncle Cardinal Fesch: Let him be sent to the first French posts at Rimini, and conveyed under escort to Paris.
tweet: I am Glad Vernegues is arrested — send him by Rimini under escort to Paris. Ignore Russian intercessions; Petersburg never approved them. Bribed intriguers meddle where they should not — pack him off at once.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The idea is to hand over this portfolio, into which the First Consul will put all the information he wishes to be beheved. But in order that a great importance should be attached to this portfolio, at least 50,000/. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To his grand-judge Régnier: Portfolio bait: planted information.
tweet: Drake letters matter most. Feed his bulletin this: the Committee delights in my Boulogne embarkation, but now sees costly feints — launches convertible to merchantmen — and a commander too secure to risk masses of troops. Ireland is the real blow.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “For the last week we have been in pursuit of forty brigands composed of Georges and his band, who disembarked at three different places. Another band is to disembark; we have arrested all the men who were to make signals. Savary awaits them at Biville. […]”

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The pleasure experienced by the people of Paris at this arrest does them credit”

context: Paris. To Marshal Soult: The pleasure experienced by the people of Paris at this arrest does them credit.
tweet: You have no doubt heard that Pichegru was arrested yesterday. He was unable to make use of his pistols or of his sabre. He fought with his fists for half an hour with three or four gendarmes. The pleasure experienced by the people of Paris at this arrest does them credit.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That the King of England would not sanction any exchange without appending unusual and arbitrary conditions. It is my intention that no flag of truce should be received at Toulon. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To his navy minister Decrès: That the King of England would not sanction any exchange without appending unusual and arbitrary conditions.
tweet: Nelson offers Latouche a prisoner exchange — tell me your answer. But no exchange: England king always appends impossible conditions. No flags of truce at Toulon.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Due d'Enghien is to be taken to the castle of Vincennes, where arrangements have been made for his reception. The First Consul desires that the name of this prisoner, and everything concerning him, may be kept secret. he travels under the name of Plessis. […]”

tweet: My orders tonight: Ordener for Strasbourg under a false name — to Ettenheim, to seize Enghien, Dumouriez and their English colonel. Caulaincourt takes 200 dragoons to Offenburg for the Reich woman and the other English agents.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The First Consul desires that the name of this prisoner, and everything concerning him, may be kept secret. he travels under the name of Plessis. " BONAPARTE." The commandant of Vincennes was also ordered to keep everything a profound secret. […]”

tweet: I am sending Enghien to Vincennes — everything prepared, everything secret, travelling as Plessis. The commandant himself must not know his prisoner name.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Receive their complaints, inspect their arms, and make sure that they want for nothing. There is a great advantage in holding these inspections of seven or eight hours; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: La Malmaison. To Marmont: There is a great advantage in holding these inspections of seven or eight hours.
tweet: I want you among the soldiers in detail — inspect them man by man, eight hours at a stretch. Hear complaints, check arms, want for nothing. Long inspections teach endurance and prove the chief shares the hardship.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Madame and dear Sister,— I have learned with pain that you have not the good sense to conform to the manners and customs of the city of Rome; that you show contempt for the inhabitants, and that your eyes are unceasingly turned towards Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Paris. To Pauline Borghese: I have learned with pain that you have not the good sense to conform to the manners and customs of the city of Rome.
voice: @borghese I have learned with pain that you have not the good sense to conform to the manners and customs of the city of Rome
tweet: It pains me you scorn Rome people and customs, eyes forever on Paris. Amid vast affairs I still speak: love your husband and his house, live Roman, shun bad counsel — or count on no support from me, Paris least of all.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I thank your Holiness for having given a cardinal's hat to the Archbishop of Bologna. I have come to the determination to take into my own hands all that relates to the Concordat with the Italian Republic. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Invitation to Paris: crown me.
tweet: I thank your Holiness for having given a cardinal's hat to the Archbishop of Bologna. I have come to the determination to take into my own hands all that relates to the Concordat with the Italian Republic.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have already received petitions signed by 30,000 soldiers, and it is for this reason that I am not with the army at present." Count Miot de Melito throws doubt upon this story; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

voice: I have already received petitions signed by 30,000 soldiers, and it is for this reason that I am not with the army at present
tweet: The councils and great bodies demand an end to Bourbon hopes — sound the army on making it hereditary. The nation made me great and powerful; I want nothing more, only her interest. My brother Joseph, major of the Revolution, burns to soldier.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Steube, the minister of Wirtemberg, is a downright fool, as ill-meaning as ignorant. If you can insinuate in a delicate manner that he ought to be recalled, that would please me. " Write to General Lannes at Lisbon, and mention the matter to M. […]”

displayText: “Write to General Lannes at Lisbon, and mention the matter to M. de Souza here, so that the Portuguese minister at Berlin, who is our bitter enemy, may be recalled. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain

tweet: Steube of Württemberg is an ignorant fool — hint delicately he should be recalled; it would please me. Write Lannes at Lisbon, tell Souza here: the Portuguese minister at Berlin, our bitter enemy, must go.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I desire that the official note of Lord Hawkesbury may be sent to all our agents at foreign courts, those of Russia, Sweden, Denmark, and the Porte excepted, with remarks to this effect — that the French Government calls attention to the note in question; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Consolidating the throne.
tweet: Send Hawkesbury's note to all my agents save Russia, Sweden, Denmark, Porte, with my gloss: gross as its insults run, contempt were my due reply, but England's open maxims overturn Europe's order and must be answered.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That no matter how gross the insults contained in it against the Government and the French nation, the French Government ought to have treated it with sovereign contempt; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: That no matter how gross the insults contained in it against the Government and the French nation, the French Government ought to have treated it with sovereign contempt.
tweet: I want Hawkesbury note circulated to every court but Russia, Sweden, Denmark and the Porte: France notes the insults with sovereign contempt — But England proclaimed principles subvert all Europe order, and that deserves answering.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “But for this miserable trial [of Moreau, &c.] I should be in the midst of the camps. I hope everything will be finished in a week. I suppose that in camp as. well as in Paris there are rumours of a continental war. This would be unfortunate, as it would turn our attention from England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Marshals for the Empire.
tweet: This wretched Moreau trial keeps me from the camps. I hope it ends within days. Camp and Paris buzz of a continental war; that would be fatal, turning us from England. Woe to war-seekers! Germany, Austria, Prussia stand with us.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “These vases must be placed at the disposal of the Cardinal Archbishop, as a gift made by the Emperor to the metropolitan church of Paris. These silver vases, fourteen in number, had been taken from the church of Tournay. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To Marshal Soult: These vases must be placed at the disposal of the Cardinal Archbishop, as a gift made by the Emperor to the metropolitan church of Paris.
tweet: But for Moreau miserable trial I would be in the camps. Give the Cardinal Archbishop my fourteen Tournay silver vases for Paris church.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I desire that you will give me by return of post some information on the subject of the family of the Elector of Bavaria, especially concerning his daughter, and his intentions with regard to that young princess. I need hardly remind you that an affair of this nature must be kept perfectly secret. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: England watched through Paris.
tweet: I desire that you will give me by return of post some information on the subject of the family of the Elector of Bavaria, especially concerning His Daughter, and his intentions with regard to that young princess.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Madam and dear Wife, — For the last four days since I have been absent from you I have been constantly on horseback, and this exercise has not impaired my health. " M. Maret tells me that you intend starting on Monday. Travelling by easy stages you will be able to reach the waters without fatigue. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: From the invasion coast.
tweet: Madam and dear Wife, for the last four days since I have been absent from you I have been constantly on horseback, and this exercise has not impaired my health. M. Maret tells me that you intend starting on Monday.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I thought boat and crew lost, but we managed to save everything. The spectacle was grand; the alarm guns, the coast in a blaze of fire, the sea tossed with fury, and roaring. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Empress Josephine, Pont  de  Briques, 1804-07-21

voice: I thought boat and crew lost, but we managed to save everything
tweet: Four days in the saddle and my health holds. Maret says you leave Monday — easy stages to the waters. Last night gale drove a gunboat ashore; we saved all, amid alarm guns and burning coasts.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “1 On the subject of the Due d'Enghien, " I suppose that you have given instructions to rayminister in America with respect to the conduct he should […]”

context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Enghien: instructions to America.
tweet: On Enghien: I take it you instructed my man in America on his conduct there. See that he follows it.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “That it is not just, by this equivocal conduct, for Austria to keep 300,000 men with arms folded, on the shores of the Channel; […]”
sourceTitle: To M. De Talleyrand, Pont  de  Briques, 1804-08-01

tweet: My health is restored — I require you to live long years yet. I am satisfied with all I have seen. Paris exaggerates our gale losses; tell our agents the army stands strong and I pass whole days drilling it.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I see by the Gazette de France that Dessalines has created a legion of honour. It will be well to verify this, and see if it is not a bad joke on the part of a journalist. […]”

voice: I see by the Gazette de France that Dessalines has created a legion of honour
tweet: Dessalines makes a legion of honour, I hear — verify whether some journalist beard pranks us.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We are convinced that this dishonourable act is the personal affair of the officer Wright and of Lord Hawkesbury, who himself drew 40,000/. […]”

voice: We are convinced that this dishonourable act is the personal affair of the officer Wright and of Lord Hawkesbury, who himself drew 40,000
tweet: My answer to Gravina: Wright was caught landing Jean Marie and two cutthroats. Three times he put brigands ashore to murder France chief magistrate — with Hawkesbury 40,000 behind him. Gallant officers would never so stain their flag.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love, I hope to hear shortly that the waters have done you very much good. I am pained that you have met with so many annoyances. I desire that you should write me often. My health is very good, although I ain a little fatigued. […]”

context: Boulogne waters: hoping they do her good.
tweet: My love, I hope to hear shortly that the waters have done you very much good. I am pained that you have met with so many annoyances. I desire that you should write me often. My health is very good, although I am a little fatigued.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love, I have been at Calais since midnight. I think of setting out this evening for Dunkirk. I am satisfied with what I see, and am in very good health. I hope that the waters may benefit you, as much as the bustle, the sight of camps, and the ocean have me. Eugene has gone to Blois. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain

tweet: My love, I have been at Calais since midnight. I think of setting out this evening for Dunkirk. I am satisfied with what I see, and am in very good health. I hope that the waters may benefit you, as much as the bustle, the sight of camps, and the ocean have me.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think it necessary to mention this, in order that you may no longer be the dupe of his assumed openness. Talleyrand was then ordered to draw up a note complaining of the conduct of Russia, and the tone of the despatches received from St. […]”

context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Talleyrand was then ordered to draw up a note complaining of the conduct of Russia, and the tone of the despatches received from St.
tweet: Mention Petersburg vileness wherever useful — an Emperor who rewards his father murderer, an ambassador false to the bone. They must stop taking me for a dupe; Talleyrand has orders for a note on Russia.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have not inspected a single regiment which has not received 100 lame conscripts, sickly and quite unfit for service. They remain in the depots, constitute a dead loss, wear out their uniforms, and cost money. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To General Lacuile: I have not inspected a single regiment which has not received 100 lame conscripts, sickly and quite unfit for service.
tweet: I find in every regiment a hundred lame, sickly conscripts — dead loss rotting in depots, wearing uniforms, costing money. And substitutes desert the moment they are paid.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Madame, — I was much pleased with your letter. The recollection of your mother and of yourself have always interested me. […]”
sourceTitle: To M. Cambacfiris, Pont  de  Briques, 1804-08-14

context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To M. Cambacfiris: The recollection of your mother and of yourself have always interested me.
voice: @cambacfiris I was much pleased with your letter
tweet: Your letter pleased me — your mother memory and you interest me always. I shall help your brother when I can. But you live near Lyons and never came to see me while I was there — I reproach you for it.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Napoleon." 1 Several despatches were exchanged on the subject of the recognition of the Emperor of Germany as hereditary Emperor of Austria, and the etiquette to be observed between the two Emperors. […]”
sourceTitle: To M. Talleyrand, Pont  de  Briques, 1804-08-14

context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Several despatches were exchanged on the subject of the recognition of the Emperor of Germany as hereditary Emperor of Austria…
tweet: Vienna needs my recognition, not I hers — Russia and Prussia will smart. I yield nothing to Germany Emperor; I recognize him as Austria Emperor only if he recognizes me first.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The note complained of the protection afforded by Russia to imigrh. M. de Markoff, when Russian minister in Paris, had openly encouraged the migrh and other agents in the pay of England; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To his foreign minister Talleyrand: Markoff feted émigrés in Russian pay.
tweet: Give Oubril his note — passports if he wants them, but he leaves Paris only when my man crosses into Russia. Markoff openly fondled émigrés in English pay, and Russia mourns a condemned conspirator.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Brother, — On recognising my house as Imperial, the House of Austria wished in its turn to be recognised as the Imperial House of Austria. […]”
sourceTitle: To The King Of Prussia, Camp  of  Arras, 1804-08-30
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To the Prussian king: On recognising my house as Imperial, the House of Austria wished in its turn to be recognised as the Imperial House of Austria.
tweet: Sir, my Brother — on recognising my house as imperial, Austria wished the same for hers. This lets me tell you how much more I value Prussia conduct, and that through Arberg I pledge myself to your crown splendour.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “D'Oubril has gone. Although this departure is not good news, still it does not mean a rupture; but it is incalculable what may happen within two or three months. "Napoleon." And on the same day Fouche was ordered not to allow any Russians to leave Paris without haying paid their debts. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: The fleet must be ready.
tweet: I d'oubril has gone. Although this departure is not good news, still it does not mean a rupture; but it is incalculable what may happen within two or three months. And on the same day Fouche was ordered not to allow any Russians to leave Paris without having paid their debts.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “And, if you were ready to transport i,000 men and 500 horses to Ireland, the result would be fatal for our enemies. […]”
sourceTitle: To Vice-Admiral Ganteaume, Aix  la  Chapelle, 1804-09-01

tweet: I want you ready to carry a thousand men and five hundred horses to Ireland -- fatal to our enemies.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “And permit me to add that everything which can contribute to the internal happiness of your family are events which will never be foreign to my own welfare. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Emperor Of Austria, Mayence, 1804-09-01

context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To the Austrian emperor: And permit me to add that everything which can contribute to the internal happiness of your family are events which will never be foreign to my own welfare.
tweet: Your kind letter moves me — congratulations on the Imperial house of Austria. Long reign and lasting peace between us; your family happiness is never foreign to my welfare. My harmony and esteem are constant.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Most Holy Father, — The happy effect which the re-establishment of the Christian religion has had on the morality and character of my people induces me to ask your Holiness to give a new proof of the interest you take in my destiny, and in that of this great nation, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Coronation details settled.
tweet: Holy Father, restored faith has remade my people's morals. Crown my work: come anoint the first French Emperor yourself. Your hands lend heaven's light; our peoples draw the Almighty's blessing on our decrees.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Vessels of war are not merchant ships. It is honour which I wish to preserve, and not a few pieces of wood and some men. […]”
sourceTitle: To His Holiness The Pope, I'^th, 1804-09-10
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To His Holiness The Pope: Vessels of war are not merchant ships.
tweet: Religion return has remade my people morals — come crown its work yourself. Anoint and crown the first French Emperor; your hand gives the lustre, and heaven blessing falls on us all.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “What happens at Bordeaux happens at Turin, at Spa, at Marseilles, &c. The police commissioners derive immense profits from the gaming-tables. My intention is that the towns shall reap the benefit of the tables. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Police on the Rhine tour.
tweet: Everywhere my police farmers coin money from gaming tables. I mean the towns to profit instead; Bordeaux tables yield two hundred thousand francs for a bridge or canal. To Berthier: Ireland is decided.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Cousin, — The expedition to Ireland has been decided upon. You will have a conference on this subject with Marshal Angereau. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: The Pope, the eagles, the new throne. To his police minister Fouché: The expedition to Ireland has been decided upon.
voice: @fouche You will have a conference on this subject with Marshal Angereau
tweet: Your commissioners coin money from gaming tables everywhere. Let the towns keep it — I grant Bordeaux 200,000 francs for a bridge or canal.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Sir, my Uncle and Cousin, — General Cafferelli is the bearer of the enclosed letter for the Pope. The Holy Father will travel in his own carriages to the foot of Mont Cenis; arrived there, my carriages will bring him on. All his expenses will be paid from the moment he sets foot in France. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Family cardinal managed.
